explanation:
**What the inputs contain.** Each input is a 15×15 black grid with four separate 3×3 blocks. Each block is filled completely with coloured cells. The output is always 3×3, and the fact sheet confirms it is an exact crop of one of the four blocks. So the task is to work out which block gets chosen.

**Comparing the blocks.** I counted the distinct colours inside each block:

| Pair | Blocks (colours used) | Chosen |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | {5,6,8}, {9,4}, {3,2}, {1,7} | {5,6,8} |
| 2 | {9,8}, {7,4}, {1,3,2}, {3,6} | {1,3,2} |
| 3 | {7,5}, {1,6,2}, {8,3}, {9,4} | {1,6,2} |

In every pair, three blocks use exactly two colours and one block uses three. The chosen block is always the three-colour one. Rule: **output the block with the most distinct colours.**

**Test input.** The blocks are {3,6}, {7,1}, {8,5} and {9,4,2}. Only the bottom-left block (rows 8–10, columns 2–4) has three colours. So the answer is:


**Construction.** I find the blocks as multicolour connected objects, because the black background separates them. Then I count the distinct colours in each block and crop the one with the highest count. The program emits two stages: first the chosen block outlined in place on the input, then the final crop.
code:
def transform(grid):
    g = np.array(grid)
    bg = background(g)
    objs = objects(g, bg=bg, multicolour=True)
    def ncol(o):
        y0, x0, y1, x1 = o["box"]
        return len(set(np.unique(g[y0:y1+1, x0:x1+1]).tolist()) - {bg})
    best = max(objs, key=lambda o: (ncol(o), o["size"]))
    y0, x0, y1, x1 = best["box"]
    # stage: show the selected block kept in place, others cleared
    marked = np.full_like(g, bg)
    marked[y0:y1+1, x0:x1+1] = g[y0:y1+1, x0:x1+1]
    emit(marked, f"Block at rows {y0}-{y1}, cols {x0}-{x1} uses {ncol(best)} colours; the others use fewer, so keep only it.")
    out = crop(g, y0, x0, y1, x1)
    emit(out, "Crop the selected block as the output.")
    return out
